newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Amsterdam airport plans to expand into North Sea.
newsitem.headline: Amsterdam airport plans to expand into North Sea.

text.p: Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport on Tuesday unveiled its choice of three offshore locations aimed at meeting its need for increased capacity in the new millennium.

Schiphol president Hans Smits said the preferred option to emerge from its feasibility study was the construction of additional remote runways on an artificial island in the North Sea some 10 kilometres off the coast.
"We think that a leap of quality in the direction of the North Sea is the most valuable option for the future," Smits told a news conference.

The other two options are the construction of a fully-fledged second airport on a purpose-created polder in the country's Markermeer lake or an overflow location for charter, freight and low-cost carriers as part of Rotterdam's industrial expansion on the Maasvlakte polder.
Government-imposed environmental norms have set a ceiling on Schiphol's growth of 44 million passengers and 3.3 million tonnes of freight a year.
But at current growth rates of around 12 percent annually, the airport, home base to Dutch national carrier KLM, is set to reach its limits by 2003 or 2004.

Further expansion of the airport has been fiercely opposed by the environmental lobby, while industry is adamant Schiphol should be allowed to grow to maintain the Netherlands' status as a major European transport hub.
Consequently the government has initiated a four-month public debate on the long-term future of the Dutch air transport infrastructure, due to be rounded off later this month.

Smits said that the possibilities raised by the feasibility study, undertaken jointly with Rotterdam's municipal port authority, engineering consultancy DHV and Siemens Nederland, represented Schiphol's contribution to the debate.

"However the airport should be reticent about opting for one or other solution, because finally it is up to society to make the choice and even this (remote runway) option has its disadvantages," Smits said.
One of these was the cost, which would run to some 29-32 billion guilders including the construction of an underground monorail link to the island, he said.
"The cost makes some form of public-private finance imperative," Smits said, but declined to put a figure on the amount Schiphol would like to see funded from the public purse.
"We have made no analyses as to the sum which should be financed from public sources," he said.
Smits said that a controversial fifth runway currently under construction at the airport would allow Schiphol to grow to 60 million passengers annually at its current location.

But the existing location would never support 80 million passengers and seven million tonnes of freight a year as outlined in Dutch civil aviation growth scenarios commissioned by the government, he said.
Smits pleaded for new legislation to speed up town and country planning processes, which can take 10 years or more.

Once a satisfactory solution for increasing airport capacity had been decided, the government could temporarily raise the capacity threshold for Schiphol's existing location until the new location was complete, he said.
"Given the prospect of a new location, I think that temporarily raising the threshold of 44 million passengers a year will be considered acceptable," he said.
-- Lien van der Leij, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000.,
